does: Builds a dish in even layers, so that it cooks evenly and holds together when it is served.

intro.what: Layering builds a dish in even sheets of its different parts.
intro.why: It helps you distribute thickness and seasoning throughout a dish rather than concentrating them on top.

how: Have every part ready and within reach before you start.
Spread each layer to the edges, in one even thickness.
Season lightly between the layers, not only on top.
Finish with the layer that should brown.

cues.text: A level top, and layers of the same thickness when the dish is cut.

mistakes.mistake: Thick and thin patches, which cook at different speeds.
mistakes.fix: Take a moment to level each layer.

mistakes.mistake: Seasoning only the top, which leaves the inside bland.

quiz.question: Why make each layer an even thickness?
choices: To make stirring during cooking unnecessary in every layered dish.
To keep the flavours of the layers from mixing at all.
To help the dish cook evenly.
quiz.because: Thick and thin patches cook at different speeds. Even layers help the dish cook evenly.

quiz.question: How should each layer be spread?
choices: To the edges in an even thickness.
In a tall mound at the centre.
In thin patches with gaps between them.
quiz.because: Spread each layer to the edges at an even thickness, rather than leaving a mound in the centre.

quiz.question: Which appearance matches the intended result?
choices: A steep mound with thin edges.
A level top and evenly thick layers in a cut portion.
quiz.because: A level top and layers of similar thickness show that the filling has been spread evenly.

quiz.question: The inside tastes bland although the top is seasoned. What would you change next time?
choices: Season only the final layer more heavily.
Season only the bottom before adding the other layers.
Season lightly between the layers as you build.
quiz.because: Seasoning only the top leaves the inside bland. Season lightly between layers as you build.
